topic: planning a weekly farmers market stall and winning back the early trade

provenance.author: glowny-en-a
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is stall-sheet arithmetic on the same stock lines with closed task questions, base is a diagnosis of slow Saturday setup and a bunching queue. Grounded external referent: the van, introduced in turn 0 and carried through the whole diagnosis (its packing order is the fault, the fix is a fixed loading list painted inside its doors).

a: Here are five lines of stock for the stall sheet, and their crate counts need adding in order.
The bread line has six crates and the apple line has five crates on the sheet.
The carrot line has four crates, and the egg line has three crates from the same shed.
The jam line is the smallest of the five at two crates for the week.
How many crates do the five lines come to when every count is added together?
base: Our Saturday stall keeps missing the early trade, and the first hour is where the money is.
We pick and pack on Friday night, then load everything into the van before dawn.
The van takes eighteen crates and the table boards, with the awning poles tied along one side.
By the time the stall stands ready, the keenest buyers have walked past to other stands.
Where does a slow market morning usually lose its first and most costly half hour?

a: Added in order, the running counts are six, then eleven, then fifteen crates so far.
The last two entries bring the count to eighteen and then twenty crates in all.
At forty pounds of takings for each crate, the bread line carries two hundred forty pounds.
The apple line carries two hundred pounds at that same forty pound rate for each crate.
Does the crate total of twenty match the number written on the Friday packing sheet?
base: The first half hour nearly always goes to setup jobs that could have happened the night before.
Awning first, table second, crates last is the order that keeps helpers out of each other's way.
Most stalls lose time hunting for things buried behind whatever was loaded last at night.
Pack the van in reverse, so the awning comes off the doors first at the site.
Which pieces come off your van first at the moment, the poles or the crates?

a: Now work out the float coins for each line at five pounds for every crate carried.
List the float for all five lines in the bread to jam order given above.
Paper bags go with each line at twenty bags for every crate on the sheet.
Put the bread and apple lines on the front table and the other three lines behind.
Which float figure belongs to the carrot line at that fixed rate of five pounds?
base: The crates come off first at the moment, because they go in last with the doors shut behind them.
The van gets packed by whoever finishes picking first, so the order changes every single week.
The awning poles end up under the table boards more often than not on busy Fridays.
Our price board rides loose on top and it has cracked twice already this year.
Would a fixed loading list pinned in the van really save us that half hour?

a: The bread line takes thirty pounds of float at the stated rate of five pounds.
The apple line takes twenty-five pounds, and the carrot line takes an even twenty pounds.
The egg line takes fifteen pounds, and the jam line takes ten pounds to finish.
The front table therefore carries fifty-five pounds of float across its two big lines.
The back lines carry forty-five pounds between them, and their bags come to one hundred eighty.
base: A fixed list saves most of it, because the saving comes from never having to think.
Write the list once: poles by the doors, boards next, then crates in selling order.
The last crates in should be the first things sold, your bread and the soft fruit.
Give the price board a flat home between the table boards where nothing can land on it.
Then make one person the packer every week, and let the van carry the same map every Friday.

a: One correction before we go on: the egg line holds four crates, not three this week.
Recalculate its float and its bags, and leave the other four lines exactly as they stand.
Then give the new totals for crates and for float across all five lines together.
After that, list the lines in the order they go onto the tables at dawn.
Which line goes out first under the order bread, then eggs, then apples, then carrots?
base: We tried the list on Saturday and the stall stood ready twenty minutes sooner than usual.
The awning came off clean, the boards followed, and the bread crates rolled straight to the front.
The van now carries a chalk line for every slot, so the packer cannot go wrong.
Even so, the queue bunched at the till while the scales sat idle at the other end.
Should the till and the scales stand together or apart when the rush comes on?

a: With four crates the egg line takes twenty pounds of float at the same rate.
Its bags become eighty, and the crate total across the five lines rises to twenty-one.
The new float total comes to one hundred five pounds across the whole stall.
The laying order stands as bread, then eggs, then apples, then carrots, then jam last.
The bread line therefore goes out first, and the jam line closes the setting out.
base: Keep the scales beside the till, because every weighed sale ends with someone paying anyway.
Put them at the end the buyers reach last, so the queue pulls people along the stall.
Display runs high at the back and low at the front, with prices facing the walkway.
One of you serves, one weighs and takes money, and nobody crosses behind the other.
A queue that moves is the best advertisement a small stand ever gets on a cold morning.

a: Convert the twenty-one crates into van slots that take three crates in each slot.
Tell me how many full slots that fills and how many crates ride loose.
Then split the float into two even tins and give the figure for each tin.
Loading starts at five in the morning with slots going in five minutes apart.
How many full slots do twenty-one crates come to at three for every slot?
base: We split the jobs on Saturday and the queue stopped folding back across the walkway.
Takings for the first hour were up by a third against a plain week last month.
The market office has offered us a corner pitch with walkway on two open sides.
It costs eight pounds more each week and sits nearer the car park entrance.
Is a corner pitch worth the extra money for a stand the size of ours?

a: Twenty-one crates fill seven full slots exactly, with no crates left riding loose at all.
Each of the two float tins holds fifty-two pounds fifty when the total splits evenly.
The first slot goes in at five o'clock and the second at five past five.
The third goes in at ten past, the fourth at quarter past, the fifth at twenty past.
The sixth slot goes in at twenty-five past, and the seventh closes the loading at half past.
base: A corner doubles your frontage, and frontage is what turns walkers into buyers on market day.
Near the car park you catch people twice, once arriving with plans and once leaving with change.
Eight pounds is one loaf and one bag of apples, which a corner should return by nine.
Take it for a month and keep the first hour takings written down for every week.
If the third and fourth Saturdays hold the gain, the corner has paid its own way.

a: Write out a four step morning sheet for the family in the order set down here.
Step one is loading, step two is the drive, step three is setting the tables.
Step four is the pricing, and every step needs its clock time on the sheet.
Loading begins at five and the tables must stand ready by seven o'clock sharp.
The drive takes forty minutes and the pricing takes ten minutes for the whole stall.
base: We have taken the corner pitch for four weeks starting with the first Saturday of the month.
My wife keeps the takings book now, one line for each hour of every market day.
The loading list is painted inside the van doors where no Friday rain can reach it.
We are adding a second small table for jams so the corner frontage does not sit bare.
The awning gets new ties as well, since the old ones frayed through last winter.

a: Step one runs from five until half past five, covering all seven slots in turn.
Step two runs from half past five until ten past six on a clear road.
Step three runs from ten past six until ten to seven for the two tables.
Step four runs from ten to seven until seven, with the board priced and faced out.
The morning sheet then closes with the stall standing ready as the first buyers arrive.
base: That takings book will settle the corner question with numbers instead of feelings inside a month.
Stock the jam table shallow and wide, because height on a corner blocks the second walkway.
Keep the bread at the point of the corner where both streams of walkers can see it.
Watch which hour empties each crate, and shift Friday picking to match what actually sells.
By the end of the month the stall should run to a rhythm the whole family knows.
